answer: Four objects chain together. `pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter>` sets the actual limit on one instance: `add`/`set` with `low-threshold` and `high-threshold` (uint64/int64/decimal64, or na / not-supported; default na). `direction` is ingress, egress, all or na (default all) and `location` is all, na, near-end or far-end (default all). `pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>` holds the per-resource-type values and exposes `default-low-threshold`, `default-high-threshold`, `min-value` and `max-value`, e.g. `set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200`. `pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>` must have `tca-supervision true` for the crossing to be reported, and `data-supervision true` for the data to be collected; `show` on it also lists `supported-parameters` (max 100 elements). `pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-tca-supervision` sets that for newly created resources.

Three objects. `set ntp ntp-enabled true` (default true) and `set ntp ntp-auth-enabled true` (default false); `assignment-method` is manual, dhcp or both (default both). Then `add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <value> key-value <value> [is-trusted <value>]` where key-id is 1..65534, key-type is sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 or md5, key-value is a string of length 8..40, and `is-trusted` defaults to false, e.g. `add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera`. Then `add ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <key-id>` (IPv4, IPv6 or DNS name; `auth-key-id` default not-applicable; `origin` manual or dhcp, default manual; `admin-state` default unlock). To verify: `show ntp ntp-active-server`, and `show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>` for `auth-status` (ok, yes, bad, none), `reach` (377 means all recent probes answered), `stratum`, `offset`, `delay`, `jitter` and `condition`. `show clock time-source` should read ntp.

They act on different things. `protection-switch` is the operating command for protection group switching: `protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<value> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>`, Operational mode. `operation-type` is force, lockout, manual or release; `switch-target` is not needed for the release and lockout operations. Example: `protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection`. The group itself is defined by `protection-group-<name>` (protection-type y-cable or snc-n, working-pu, protection-pu, reliable-cp), whose `pg-request` and `pg-state` reflect the switch. `manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<AID>` is the controller command: it moves the active controller card, e.g. `manual-switchover card-1-3`, and warns 'Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost. Do you want to continue? [y/n]'. Use `-f` to skip the confirmation.

`set-time` is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled, so an enabled NTP is what rejects it. Check `show clock time-source`: values are ntp (NE synchronises via NTP) and manual (NE internal clock), default manual. `show clock` also gives `current-time`, `universal-time`, `timezone` (default Universal-Time-Coordinated), `DST-active` and `last-time-jump` (jumps under 10 seconds are ignored). `time` prints the current system time in the configured timezone. If you really want manual time, `set ntp ntp-enabled false` first; otherwise fix the source with `show ntp ntp-active-server` and `show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>` (`reach` 377 means all recent probes answered, plus `stratum`, `offset`, `auth-status`, `condition`). `set-time` format is ISO 8601 combined date and time, `set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z` for UTC or `set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00` for an offset.

Identity: `show ne` gives `ne-id`, `ne-name` (default '1830 GX'), `ne-type` (G30 or G40), `node-type` (ILA, OADM, XPDR), `ne-site`, `ne-location`, `clli`, `node-controller-chassis-name` (default 1), `equipment-discovery-ready`, `alarm-report-ready` and `recover-mode`. Contents: `show equipment`, `show slot` (supported-type, installed-type, current-equipment), `show inventory`, `show card-<name>`, and the `status` / `status equipment` dashboards. Cost: `restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]`, Operational mode, requires confirmation unless `-f`. With no resource-id it restarts the active controller card. `type` defaults to warm. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, connectivity returns within five minutes (cold on XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost); warm reboots only the processor and is non service affecting (XMM4 loses visibility for 3 minutes); shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. Sub-components are listed by `show card resources`.

The chassis holds `slot` and `inventory`, so slot 2 is `slot-1-2` (`show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>` gives AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state, current-equipment) and the card provisioned there is `card-<name>` created with `add card-<name> required-type <value> chassis-name <value> slot-name 2`. Beneath a `card` hang `comm-eth`, `inventory`, `port`, `property`, `sub-component`, `tom` and `usb`. Beneath a `port` hang `current-fw`, `serdes` and `supported-tom-power`. The pluggable itself is `tom-<card-name>-<port-name>` (`add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD`), and its FRU data is read with `show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>`, e.g. `show inventory-1-3-1`, giving hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class (uint8, range 1..8), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status.

Capability of the model is `supported-card`: `show supported-card-<card-type>` returns `supported-subtype`, `default-card-mode`, `supported-card-mode`, `card-width` (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), `card-height` in RUs, `category` (controller, line-card, fan, power-supply, other, carrier-card, blank), `is-field-replaceable`, `max-power-draw` in Watts, `node-type-compatibility` (all, ILA, OADM), `grid-mode-support` (default general-c-band), `supported-bands` (default standardC-band), `console-port-support`, `support-serdes-config` and `location-led-support`. Its ports, slots and pluggables are `supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>`, `supported-slot` and `supported-tom`. The card actually fitted is `card-<name>`: `show card-1-7` gives required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, power-profile, category, chassis-name, slot-name, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, admin-state, oper-state and avail-state. `show capabilities-<name>` retrieves a specific card's capabilities.

The stack must be built bottom-up. `ospf-instance-<instance-id>` (id 0..255) needs `router-id`; `router-id-mode` is manual or use-loopback, default use-loopback, and the stated pre-condition is that with use-loopback an ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. `version` is ospfv2 (default) or ospfv3. `ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>` has the pre-condition that the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added; `ospf-area-type` is normal. `ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>` has the pre-condition that the instance and the area must be present; `enable` defaults true, `hello-interval` default 10, `router-dead-interval` default 40, `ospf-cost` default 10, `priority` default 1. Then `show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id>` shows how far it got: state down, init, 2-way, exstart, exchange, loading, full, plus role drother/dr/bdr/ptp. Its pre-condition is that the neighbour NEs also have instance, area and interface configured and are connected with DCN interface bridges; an OSPF neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface goes down.

`show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>` is the per-card view, where location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> and swload-state is active, inactive or installable, e.g. `show software-load-1-5/active`. It returns swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status, swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-pkg-type. The pieces inside it are `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>` giving state (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown; default unknown), version and description, e.g. `show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg`, and one level down `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>`. The bundled firmware is `show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name>` with `fw-version`; versions for the same firmware can differ per equipment-type. `swversion` lists active, inactive and installable versions.

Work per port with three show commands. `show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port>` is what this node advertises: chassis-id-subtype chassis-component with the chassis serial number as chassis-id, port-id-subtype local with the port AID as port-id, port-description (the port name), system-name (the NE name) and system-description. `show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/<direction>` is what was received; direction is ingress only, the egress direction is not supported. It gives last-update, age, ttl, chassis-id, port-id, system-name and capabilities, and is kept indefinitely until the port is decommissioned or cleared. `show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/ingress` separates sending from receiving: total-frames-out, total-frames-in, error-frames, total-discarded-frames, total-discarded-tlvs, total-unrecognized-tlvs, total-ageouts, last-change-time, last-clear-time, all defaulting to 0. These counters freeze whenever lldp-admin-status is disabled for that port. `show lldp hold-on-timer` is the global neighbour retention time, default 900 seconds, used when the neighbour sends no TTL TLV.

`show slot` (or `show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>`, e.g. `show slot-1-1`) lists every holder with AID, `supported-type`, `installed-type`, `oper-state`, `avail-state` and `current-equipment`; an empty installed-type and a current-equipment of --- mean nothing is fitted. `show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>` gives the FRU data for whatever is in it: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, actual-power-class, actual-max-power-draw, and `fw-status` (not-applicable, current, not-current, unavailable; default not-applicable). Firmware level is `show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name>` (also addressable per card and per port), returning `fw-version`, `expected-fw-version` and `fw-status` (current, not-current, unavailable; default unavailable). A bare `show current-fw` prints the whole table, e.g. current-fw-1-1/CORE_BOOT 0x20 vs expected 0x28, not-current.

`show manifest-<manifest-file>` lists the downloaded manifest with `manifest-signature` (hex string up to 1024), `downloaded-on` (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ) and `information`. Contents are `show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name>`, which returns `state` (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown; default unknown), `version` and `description`, so that is where you see whether each piece got installed. Bundled firmware is `show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name>` with `fw-version`. `show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name>` shows the image files pulled down and their `signature`, and `show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>` shows the packaged FRU information for one equipment-type. Example: `show manifest-G40_BASIC-R6.1.0-F-2023.01.04_15_40-x-sim-u-1940.manifest`. For what actually landed on a card, cross-check `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>` and `show upgrade-status`.

Two profile objects keyed by resource type. Alarm severity comes from `alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location>`, whose `severity` is critical, event, major, minor, not-reported or warning, e.g. `set alarm-severity-entry-tom/EQPTCOMFAIL severity major`; direction is na, ingress or egress and location is na, near-end or far-end. `alarm-severity-profile` is the system-managed container over those entries: `set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value>`. PM defaults come from `pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>`, whose `default-data-supervision` and `default-tca-supervision` (true/false) state, verbatim, whether newly created resources of this type have PM data supervision and PM threshold crossing supervision automatically enabled. Above it `pm-profile global-data-supervision` is auto-enabled or manual (default manual), and threshold defaults live in `pm-threshold-profile` as `default-low-threshold` and `default-high-threshold`.

`ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>` is the decision: its `action` is protect, bypass or discard, default protect. `priority` (uint8) is mandatory on add and gives precedence between SPD entries; `mode` is tunnel or transport (default tunnel), `ipsec-protocol` is ESP, `esn` defaults true, `anti-replay-window` is 32..1024 default 64 and applies when action is protect, and `dynamic-ts` defaults disabled. Example: `add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect`. Underneath the SPD entry hang `ipsec-sa-proposal-.../<number>` and `ipsec-traffic-selector-.../<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>` (with `next-layer-protocol`: any = 0, opaque = 255, or 0-255, default any). Under the traffic selector hang `local-subnet`, `remote-subnet`, `local-ports` and `remote-ports`. `ipsec-sa-re-key` sits under the peer, and `security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name>` lists the associated-secure-entity.

`trusted-certificate-<id>` is the CA you trust: the X509v3 CA (Root and Intermediate) certificate trusted by the system. `local-certificate-<id>` is this node's own identity: the X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing one of the various secure application identities; it uniquely carries `used-by` (the secure-applications, ikev2-peers and so on presently using it) and `self-signed`. `peer-certificate-<id>` is the far end: the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer certificate for the L1 encryption secure application; it uniquely carries `white-listed`, true when it has no trust chain and was explicitly white-listed at import. The fourth, `certificate`, is not a per-certificate object at all but the operational command over all three: `show certificates`, `show certificate-revocation` and `clear [-f] certificate [type=]<trusted|local|peer> [id=]<value>`. All three share version v3, serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, status and `revocation-mode` (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked; default auto).

Import with `import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]`, Operational mode; the type is local-certificate, trusted-certificate or peer-certificate, e.g. `import-certificate trusted-certificate certificate-name=trusted-cert-1 <string in PEM format>`. `-i` imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM bundle, or for a single-certificate file the intermediates named by the AIA extension; root certificates must be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, for example trusted-certificate-Nokia-1. A passphrase applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. Remove with `clear [-f] certificate [type=]<trusted|local|peer> [id=]<value>`, Operational mode, which prompts 'Are you sure? [y/n]'; the id must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type, and <tab> lists the clearable ids. Bulk options are purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused.

`ace-<name>/<sequence-id>` is what permits or blocks IP traffic: its `action` is drop, accept or reject (default drop), matched on source/destination IP, L4 port ranges, `protocol` (default any), `ttl` (1..255, default 255) and `direction` (input or output, default input). Its `sequence-id` sets the relative order within the ACL. `acl-<name>` is the container that binds those entries to an interface (1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-B, DCN-2, DCN-2-B) with `type` IPv4 or IPv6; an ACL must exist before an ACE can be added. `access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name>` is not traffic filtering at all: it permits or denies management access to YANG paths, RPCs and notifications (`action` permit or deny, mandatory), while `access-rule-list-<name>` groups those rules per user-group and is processed in order by `sequence-id`. `access-control-list` is a show-only container. Further out, `sw-control-rule-<service-name>` has nothing to do with access or traffic: its `fail-action` (default-action, ignore, system-restart) governs what happens when a software service fails.

Order is by `sequence-id` (uint16) on `access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name>`: lower number ids are processed first, so the lower sequence-id wins. If sequence-id is not provided, it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, which places the rule at the end of the list. The id can be changed over the lifetime of the access-rule-list to re-sort entries. The list itself, `access-rule-list-<name>`, is a group of access-rules organised by which user-groups they apply to and is likewise processed in order by its own `sequence-id`. Its `user-group` is a leaf-list of user-group names with a maximum of 20 user-groups referenced; the default value '*' is the match-all representation, meaning the list applies to all existing user-groups. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists. For IP filtering with `ace`, the sequence-id range is 1-100 for AUX and DCN-B interfaces and 1-256 for DCN-A, recommended in multiples of 5, with a maximum of 16 ACEs per ACL when both upper-port and lower-port are specified.

The trap community string is not on `snmp-community` at all; that object explicitly notes that the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. Set it with `add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]` or with `set snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string <value>`. `trap-community-string` is a string of 0..32 characters and defaults to 'infinera', which is what a receiver expecting your own string will reject. `snmp-version` is v2c (default) or v3, `snmpv3-user` applies only when the version is v3, `target-port` is 0..65535 default 162, `target-transport` is udp, and `enabled` defaults true. `snmp-community-<name>` with its `community-string` (1..32) and `community-string-access` (read-only) governs polling access only.

`external-fiber-connection-<name>` is the one filled in by something else: the guide states it is set autonomously by TNMS, and although it is possible to configure it manually, it is not recommended to do so. It represents the physical link between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations, and takes `src-node-id`, `src-card-name`, `src-port-name`, `dst-node-id`, `dst-card-name`, `dst-port-name`, `fiber-connection-type` (one-way or two-way, default two-way) and `scope` (general-purpose or cable-id, default general-purpose; entries not scoped cable-id are excluded from the CableID path and are not verified). By contrast `fiber-connection-<name>` is the user-created intra-NE link between two distinct ports or sub-ports in the same NE, with label, src-port, dst-port and fiber-connection-type. `supporting-fiber-connection-<name>` is show-only and just returns the `fiber-connection-list` supporting an entity.

The one you want is `ipv4-address`: `add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>`, for example `add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0`. `show` adds `origin` (static, dhcp, auto-config; default static). Addresses beginning with 0, with 127, or with 224 up to 255 are disallowed, and only valid netmasks are accepted. The two look-alikes are LLDP read-only objects, not configuration. `management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address>` retrieves the management addresses advertised by the remote system and received on a local port, with `if-subtype` (unknown, if-index, system-port-number), `if-id` and `address-oid`. `management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>` is the same information for the local LLDP ports, with no direction key, and its `address-oid` is currently an empty string. Neither assigns an address to an interface.

The stated pre-condition on `ipv4-address` is that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. So check `show interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method`, which is static or dhcp (default static), and `ipv4-enabled` (true/false, default true); switch it back with `set interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method static`. The other rejections come from the address itself: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), with 127 (loopback), or with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental) are disallowed, and only valid netmasks are allowed. To see which interfaces are available, use `show interface` (which returns if-type ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp or hdlc, supporting-port, backup-port, vrf, protection-mode and admin/oper/avail-state), or type '?' after `ipv4-address-` and the system displays the object completion options.

`show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>` is the list of system routes from various sources such as dynamic protocols and static routes; `source-protocol` names the origin (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) and `special-next-hop` is none, blackhole or unreachable (default none). The table it lives in is `show rib-<rib-name>`, with `vrf` and `address-family` (ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast); for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family, e.g. `show rib-IPv4`. `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface>` gives the `next-hop-address`, e.g. `show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN`. Hand-typed routes are added with `add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]`, where `distance` is 1..255 default 1, `advertised` defaults false, and `origin` is manual or dhcp (default manual). Example: `add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165`. `ipv6-static-route` is the IPv6 equivalent.

`local-ports` and `remote-ports` are the IPsec pair. Both are keyed `<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>`, so they hang under an `ipsec-traffic-selector` inside an `ipsec-spd-entry` on an IKEv2 peer, and they define the local and remote Layer 4 port ranges the selector matches. `start` is all, opaque or a port number; `stop` defaults to 0, and 0 is only accepted when start is all or opaque. Examples: `add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53` and `add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all`. `connection-ports` is unrelated to security: `show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]` is a Layer 0 topology object that reports the dwdm-line port of the RD or ILAx card associated with a degree, and creates the OMS of the corresponding dwdm-port. `degree-number` is 1..20 and must not exceed max-degrees; `index` has range 1..2 but is always 1 in the 1830 GX since dwdm-line ports are bi-directional, e.g. `connection-ports-5/1  port-name port-4-1-dwdm-line1`.

`take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]` (Operational mode) creates the local snapshot, storing the current Configuration database into one of the backup slots. `db-instance` is temp (default, temporary storage for manual backup and restore), manual (permanent storage for important configurations), rollback, or the automatic onehour, oneday and oneweek; `type` is db-backup (default) or system-backup; `description` is up to 128 characters. It is refused if the db-passphrase used for snapshot encryption is not configured, either globally via `set security-policies db-passphrase` or as a parameter of this command; the passphrase needs a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain dictionary words, and allows special characters from the 85-character Z85 set. `activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]` puts it back, default sanity-check-override false, with the pre-condition that a snapshot must have been taken. `show database` and `show database-<database-type>` (active, manual, oneday, onehour, oneweek, rollback, temp) list them with backup-time, ne-name and description.
